newsitem.title: EGYPT: Stock markets seen boosting Africa economic reform.
newsitem.headline: Stock markets seen boosting Africa economic reform.

text.p: The growing influence and unity of African stock exchanges is reinforcing economic reforms across the continent, the chairman of the African Stock Exchange Association said on Monday.

Roy Andersen told the association's annual meeting: "There is a wave of economic freedom spreading across Africa and it is encouraging that use of African stock exchanges for economic empowerment and reconstruction and development objectives has continued to grow over the past year."

Andersen, who is also executive president of the Johannesburg Stock Exchange, said the exchanges have agreed to work together to set minimum listing requirements which would be uniform across the continent.
"A minimum threshold for listings in Africa facilitates dual listings, but also makes Africa much more attractive to foreign investors," he said.
Overseas investors would feel much more comfortable buying African shares if they knew automatically what were the minimum requirements for a company to be traded.

But he warned that all countries need to lift restrictions on foreign investment and on ownership of broking firms. "Those exchanges which have not lifted restrictions on foreign investment need to do that if they are serious about attracting foreign investment," he said.

There are 16 stock exchanges in Africa, of which six were formed in the past seven years. In 1996 at least six African countries said they planned to open exchanges -- Angola, Cameroon, Madagascar, Mozambique, Uganda and Tanzania -- and there were plans for a unified West African exchange linking Senegal, Mali, Niger, Burkina Faso, Togo and Benin.

At June 30, 1996, the market capitalisation of African exchanges exceeded $300 billion. South Africa clearly dominated the continent, representing about 98 percent of total market capitalisation. "But the imbalance between South Africa and the rest of Africa is an opportunity and not a threat. Both sides could benefit from integration," Andersen said.
Foreign investors like to spread their risks and would welcome companies listing on more than one exchange in Africa.

But the International Monetary Fund's representative in Egypt, Arvind Subramanian, told the meeting that Africa still attracts only 4.5 percent of the direct portfolio and equity investment which flows into developing economies.
"Sound economic policies are key to expanding capital inflows. Countries which adhere to these policies have been able to deepen their access to capital markets," he said.
"These policies are the prerequisite for high return/low risk outcome which is what all investors are seeking."
